An arcade is fundamentally a structure or space defined by a row of arches. Everything else the word means grew out of that single architectural idea. To understand "arcade" fully, you need to understand its three distinct meanings — all of which are connected to each other like links in a chain.

In its purest, most technical sense, an arcade is a series of arches standing side by side in a line, each arch supported by its own column or pillar underneath. Picture a long corridor where, instead of a flat ceiling or a flat wall, you have a continuous sequence of curved arches one after another — like a tunnel made of repeated rounded doorways.

You'll find this kind of arcade in old churches, cathedrals, historic public buildings, palace courtyards, and ancient ruins. The arches are not just decoration — they carry the weight of the structure above them, distributing it downward through the columns.

A special sub-type: the blind arcade
A blind arcade is a row of arches that are decorative rather than functional. The arches are carved into or attached to a solid wall — they don't open into any passage or space. They exist purely to make a plain wall look more elegant and structured. You'll commonly see blind arcades on the exterior walls of medieval churches and cathedrals.

This is the same architectural idea applied to a real-world space people walk through. A shopping arcade is a covered walkway or gallery, usually with shops on both sides, enclosed overhead by a glass roof or a decorative vaulted ceiling. It is essentially an elegant, sheltered indoor street.

These were invented in the 19th century as a way to let people shop comfortably without being exposed to bad weather. The ceiling lets in natural light while keeping out rain and cold. The sides are lined with small boutiques, cafés, or specialty shops. The whole structure often has an ornate, grand, historic feel.

Famous real-world examples include the Burlington Arcade in London and the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II in Milan — both beautiful, glass-roofed passages lined with high-end shops, still in use today.

The connection to Meaning 1 is direct: the covered passage often features actual arches along its length, and its entire design comes from that classical architectural tradition.

This is the meaning most people today are most familiar with. An amusement arcade — often just called an arcade — is a commercial venue filled with coin-operated or token-operated entertainment machines: video games, pinball machines, claw/crane machines, racing simulators, and similar games. You pay per game (or buy tokens) and play for fun, prizes, or simply the experience.

Arcades in this sense were enormously popular from the 1970s through the 1990s, when home gaming was limited and playing the latest video games meant going to a dedicated arcade. Classic arcade games like Pac-Man, Space Invaders, and Street Fighter were played this way. Though less dominant today due to home gaming and smartphones, arcades still exist in entertainment centers, shopping malls, and amusement parks around the world.

The connection to Meaning 2 is the key link here: in the 19th and early 20th centuries, covered shopping arcades began housing coin-operated amusement machines alongside their shops. Over time, some venues became dedicated entirely to those machines — and the name "arcade" came along with them.

Think of it as a natural evolution:

Arches in a row → created covered walkways → those walkways housed amusement machines → venues dedicated to those machines kept the name.

So the word "arcade" travelled from architecture → commerce → entertainment, carrying its name the whole way.

MeaningWhat it is
Architectural arcadeA row of connected arches supported by columns

Knowing all three meanings means you'll never be confused by this word, whether you encounter it in a description of a medieval cathedral, a reference to a 19th-century Parisian shopping gallery, or a conversation about classic video games.
